question: A certain sum becomes 4 times of itself in 5 years at a rate of simple interest. In 15 years it will become how many times of itself at the same rate of simple interest?
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

In Simple Interest, the interest earned is directly proportional to the time period.

Direct Formula: (n₁ − 1) ÷ t₁ = (n₂ − 1) ÷ t₂

Given: n₁ = 4, t₁ = 5 years, t₂ = 15 years.

⇒ (4 − 1) ÷ 5 = (n₂ − 1) ÷ 15

⇒ 3 ÷ 5 = (n₂ − 1) ÷ 15 ⇒ n₂ − 1 = 9 ⇒ n₂ = 10

**∴ The correct answer is 10 times.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

A sum becomes 4 times of itself in 5 years at simple interest.

**Formula Used:**

Simple Interest (SI) = (P × R × T) ÷ 100

Amount (A) = P + SI

**Calculations:**

⇒ Let the principal sum be P.

⇒ Amount after 5 years = 4P

⇒ Simple Interest earned in 5 years = 4P − P = 3P

⇒ Rate of Interest (R) = (SI × 100) ÷ (P × T)

⇒ R = (3P × 100) ÷ (P × 5) = 60%

⇒ Now, we need to find the amount after T = 15 years at R = 60%:

⇒ SI = (P × 60 × 15) ÷ 100

⇒ SI = 900P ÷ 100 = 9P

⇒ New Amount = Principal + SI = P + 9P = 10P

⇒ Thus, the sum will become 10 times of itself.

**∴ The correct answer is 10 times.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Simple Interest Constant Growth

Unlike compound interest, simple interest grows by a constant amount every year. If a sum earns 3P interest in 5 years, it will earn exactly 3P interest in every subsequent 5-year period.

Direct Formula for Multipliers

When a sum becomes n₁ times in t₁ years and n₂ times in t₂ years at simple interest, use the relation: (n₁ − 1) ÷ t₁ = (n₂ − 1) ÷ t₂.

Principal and Amount Relation

The amount (A) is the sum of Principal (P) and Simple Interest (SI). Always subtract 1 from the number of times it becomes to get the interest multiplier: SI = (n − 1)P.
